- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.
> Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website, Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday.
> The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
> A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:
> The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August, but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”
> Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules, a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”
> In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture, a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.
> OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.
> OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal r...

### Bloomberg analysis of 10 million job postings shows AI-exposed roles in China fell 10 percentage points faster than others
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/63da5ec12e3272af
- Primary Source: THE DECODER (https://the-decoder.com/bloomberg-analysis-of-10-million-job-postings-shows-ai-exposed-roles-in-china-fell-10-percentage-points-faster-than-others/)
- Executive Summary: of nearly 10 million job postings reveals that AI is significantly disrupting China's labor market, disproportionately affecting entry-level and creative roles. Vulnerable positions have seen a demand decline 10 percentage points sharper than non-impacted roles, with research from ShanghaiTech University and the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences confirming structural shifts including role consolidation and quiet staff reductions at major internet firms.
- Key Verified Facts:

* [Key Metrics] 2% in new hires between 2023 and early 2026.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Implicit headcount optimization across major tech firms amidst broader labor market headwinds.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> An analysis of 10 million job postings by Bloomberg suggests that AI is putting additional pressure on China's already weak labor market. Entry-level workers and the creative industry in particular are reportedly already feeling the shift.
> China's labor market has struggled for years with a sluggish economy, and AI now appears to be making things worse. According to a Bloomberg News analysis of nearly 10 million online job postings between July 2021 and June 2025, listings for jobs highly exposed to AI fell about 10 percentage points more than listings for less affected roles.
> Bloomberg found that the total number of online job postings halved in the three years after June 2022, a starting point shortly before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and Chinese models like DeepSeek and ByteDance's Doubao rose to prominence. In nearly every industry, the decline hit jobs harder when their tasks overlapped heavily with AI capabilities, as measured by an index from Peking University. Bloomberg acknowledges, however, that the pure AI effect cannot be isolated with certainty because the broader economic slowdown may have hit office jobs disproportionately on its own.
> ### Chinese studies back up the findings
> Two independent Chinese studies reached similar conclusions, according to Bloomberg. Data scientist Chen Qin of ShanghaiTech University analyzed 116 million online job postings and estimates that AI caused a net loss of 5.2% in new hires between 2023 and early 2026.
> A study involving the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences goes even further, finding 21% fewer online job postings and 4% lower average wages. Bloomberg Economics estimates that roughly 70 million workers in China are at risk from AI disruption, compared with about 45 million in the US.
> Chinese tech companies avoid citing AI openly as a reason for layoffs because they fear backlash from the government and the public, Bloomberg reports. Companies including Xiaomi, Meituan, and Alibaba's travel unit Fliggy have denied mass layoffs. Employees at large firms, however, have reported waves of cuts since spring that affected up to 30% of some departments.
> Previously separate roles are also merging, according to Bloomberg. One Beijing-based internet company reportedly combined programming, design, and testing so that a single person using AI would take on the work of up to six people. Job postings from Tencent for an "AI Design Engineer"and from BlueFocus for an "AI Director"point in the same direction.
> ### AI micro-dramas are replacing film crews
> According to Bloomberg, the shift is even more dramatic in Chinese micro-dramas, 90-second soap operas made for smartphones. Since the launch of new AI video generators like ByteDance's Seedance 2.0 in February, production time and costs have plummeted. Official ...

> The Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation, established by Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) co-founder Jensen Huang and his wife, plans to spend $350 million on computing time from CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV).
> The commitment is by far the foundation's largest gift last year, and an earlier Nvidia filing showed $108.3 million had already been spent. It donated about $373 million in total, roughly three times its 2024 giving.
> Warning! GuruFocus has detected 3 Warning Signs with NVDA.
> Is NVDA fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.
> The money supports the Computing Initiative for Open Science, which gives research grant recipients access to large-scale graphics processing unit, or GPU, computing power, the filing said. A CoreWeave spokesperson said the foundation does not use the computing itself, and a spokesperson for Huang declined to comment.
> The arrangement adds to concerns about circular financing, in which chip suppliers such as Nvidia invest in customers, which may create artificial demand. Nvidia is a major CoreWeave shareholder, and Huang defended the company after its shares slumped on concerns about debt-funded hardware spending.
> Its assets reached $12.7 billion at the end of 2025, up from $9.2 billion a year earlier, with Nvidia shares making up nearly 90%.

### Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says he used Claude to prove the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis and posts the proof in the Lean programming language (Joseph Howlett/Scientific American)

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Levent Alpöge, a mathematician and employee at artificial intelligence company Anthropic, claimed on Friday to have proven the most famous problem in all of mathematics using an LLM.
> “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote in a statement posted on his website.
> The Riemann hypothesis was first proposed in 1859 by the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It claims that the locations of the prime numbers along the number line, which appear random at first blush, are actually determined by an intricate, meaningful order.
> The conjecture has since become the North Star for the entire field of number theory, and is the most famous open problem in math. Progress toward solving the Riemann hypothesis was so rare that most top experts spent little of their time actually working on it, because there was no obvious path to proving Riemann’s guess. The first chink in the problem’s armor appeared in October, when one of the proofs in OpenAI’s massive dump of math results made significant progress on making sense of the primes.
> Now the long struggle appears over. Alpöge posted his Claude proof coded in the programming language Lean, which verifies the mathematical correctness of each argument. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn’t take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct.
> If that happens, it will cap off a year in which AI’s mathematical capabilities ascended from unreliable college student to a superhuman force, leaving no part of the discipline undisrupted.
> Alpöge says his proof confirms the “Generalized Riemann Hypothesis,” a gargantuan expansion on Riemann’s initial guess that undergirds the entire mathematical universe with untold hidden structure. There is no superlative strong enough for how this would transform mathematics, instantly unlocking a deluge of truths contingent upon the ambitious conjecture.
> Alpöge’s statement is elegiac—recognizing the sense of grief many mathematicians are feeling—but also optimistic. “It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light,” he wrote. “But what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.”
> The Anthropic mathematician has been the subject of headlines since he tweeted a Claude-generated solution to the famous Jacobian conjecture in July, kicking off math’s unprecedented summer.
> “I hope the argument provides a glimpse towards the miracles that lie ahead,” Alpöge wrote, “and shows us the joy and wonder we are about to find in the simplest things.”
> This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

> Anthropic PBC shares erased much of their first-day jump on Friday, testing investors’ faith after the AI lab delivered the biggest initial public offering in history.
> Shares in the company behind the Claude chatbot plunged as low as $87.26 each in early trading in its second day as a public company, trimming the gain from the IPO price of $83 to as little as 5.1%. The stock popped just after opening on Thursday, briefly lifting Anthropic’s market value above Amazon.com Inc.’s, before beginning its slide.
> The drop came at the same time as the so-called over-allotment option, also known as a greenshoe, was exercised, allowing the underwriting banks to sell additional shares. The over-allotment lifted the total raised by Anthropic and the co-founders selling shares in the offering to $119.5 billion, with $93.5 billion in the IPO and $26 billion from the concurrent private placement.
> The trading gives Anthropic a market value of about $1.5 trillion, ranking it among the 15 biggest publicly traded companies in the world. Stocks were roiled by a selloff that spread from Asia to the US, with the Nasdaq 100 Index falling 1.5% and the S&P 500 Index sinking 0.5%.
> “There’s a buyers’ strike for Anthropic as well as the wider AI and tech trade,” according to Emmanuel Valavanis of Forte Securities.
> “There are many clients who appear to have been left without allocations and, having been left out of the party, aren’t prepared to pick up the pieces from the hangover. With no skin in the game, and no index considerations for risk of relative performance, investors can sit on the sidelines and wait for longer term price discovery rather than risk getting caught out.”
> Anthropic’s IPO made history not only because of its size, but also because the company is the first frontier AI model maker to go public. The trading represents a test of whether investors have appetite for companies pioneering the technology itself, rather than the tools to develop it such as chips and data centers. It also sets up a debut for rival OpenAI, which isn’t planning to go public before 2027.
> The IPO delivered outsize returns to its backers and pushing up the combined wealth of its seven founders to $166 billion. The fundraise eclipsed the record set in June by SpaceX’s IPO, which ultimately totaled $86.2 billion. Goldman Sachs Group Inc., Morgan Stanley and 20 other banks earned a record $550 million in fees for their work on Anthropic’s IPO.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Nvidia is nearing a deal to acquire AI startup Inception for at least $500 million. That's according to three people familiar with the talks told The Information. The deal also includes performance bonuses for the more than 30 employees at the two-year-old San Francisco Bay Area startup.
> Inception builds language models using the diffusion process known from image generation. Rather than generating responses token by token like the conventional models behind ChatGPT and Claude, they refine a full response step by step. The startup most recently released Mercury 3.
> The acquisition aims to bolster Nvidia's open-source Nemotron models and physical models for robots, helping it compete with OpenAI and Anthropic as both build their own inference chips. Palantir and US government agencies already use Nemotron as an alternative to Chinese models. Talks began before Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation and after Microsoft expressed interest. Inception co-founders and professors Stefano Ermon, Aditya Grover, and Volodymyr Kuleshov are expected to join Nvidia full time. Neither company initially commented.
> We covered Inception's approach alongside 40 other neolabs in our latest AI Radar #5.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Anthropic underwriters have officially exercised their overallotment of shares in the historic initial public offering, bringing the total raised to $93.5 billion, according to a release on Friday.
> The artificial intelligence company raised $81.3 billion on Wednesday and net an additional $12.2 billion through the overallotment, surpassing SpaceX, which held a record IPO in June.
> Anthropic said it sold an aggregate of 1,127,000,000 shares of its Class A common stock at $83 per share in the offering. It sold 980 million shares on Wednesday and its underwriters had the option to purchase up to an additional 147 million shares by Friday as part of the overallotment, which is commonly referred to as the "greenshoe."
> Shares of the Claude maker opened trading at $111.50 on the Nasdaq Thursday, but slid throughout the day and closed at $97.17. The stock sank 12% in pre-market trading on Friday during a broad tech sell-off.
> In addition to the sale of its Class A common stock, Anthropic closed a concurrent sale of its Class N common stock after a group of tech companies, including Advanced Micro Devices, Google, Microsoft, Nvidia and others, agreed to participate in a $26 billion private placement at the IPO price. Anthropic said Friday that aggregate gross proceeds from its IPO, including the private placement, totaled $119.5 billion, before deducting offering expenses.
> Anthropic dodged an unforgiving series of obstacles on its road to the Nasdaq on Thursday, as investors brooded over Jensen Huang's shocking ouster at Nvidia, voters' stinging rebuke of the tech during the midterms and whether rising interest rates would stymie industry plans for a multi-trillion-dollar AI infrastructure buildout.
> CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company in 2021 after he and a handful of other researchers, including his sister Daniela, quit their jobs at OpenAI, now Anthropic's chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude, which have captivated the corporate world and fueled the company's historic rise.
> The siblings celebrated the IPO as a "milestone"in an interview with CNBC on Thursday, but said there's more work ahead for Anthropic.
> "For us, it's like one stop on the journey,"Daniela Amodei said. "We think about this as, 'Wow, this is an incredible moment for Anthropic for our mission, but we're going to wake up tomorrow and we're going to be the same company.'"

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Google is rolling out a collapsible sidebar globally on its Desktop Search homepage, making AI search even easier to access. Announced on X by Google Search VP Robby Stein, the feature lets users easily find and reopen recent AI searches. Sitting on the left side of the AI Mode interface, it lets users start new threads, search existing ones, create notebooks, and open recent queries and settings.
> Stein said people are increasingly asking Google Search questions that a single query can't answer. In testing, the sidebar significantly helped users make progress and keep researching across the web by making it easier to pick up right where they left off. The update also pushes Google's shift toward an AI answer engine.
> Google is also rolling out temporary threads in AI Mode worldwide. These searches don't use prior context, aren't saved to history, and don't affect future recommendations. Once closed, they're gone, Stein said.

### Uber tests rides for kids as young as 10, with extra pay for drivers
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/8554ccc9acbebab1
- Primary Source: TechCrunch (https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/19/uber-tests-rides-for-kids-as-young-as-10-with-extra-pay-for-drivers/)
- Executive Summary: Uber has launched the 'Uber Kids' pilot program in Austin, Nashville, and Madison, lowering the minimum ride-hailing age to 10. The service mandates parental onboarding, real-time video monitoring, PIN verification, and GPS-based off-course detection, while offering participating high-rated drivers a $7 premium per trip.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Uber Technologies Inc.: Lowered minimum age to 10 with enhanced safety protocols and driver incentives
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To capture high-frequency family transport demand and expand the service addressable market
* [Key Metrics] Supply-side incentives: $7 premium per trip to recruit and retain high-rated drivers.

The service mandates parental onboarding, real-time video monitoring, PIN verification, and GPS-based off-course detection, while offering participating high-rated drivers a $7 premium per trip.", 'key_points_zh': ['13-1710', 'PIN', '720'], 'key_points_en': ['Expanded service eligibility from 13-17 to 10-year-olds', 'Enhanced safety protocols including mandatory parental presence, real-time video, and PIN verification', 'Supply-side incentives: $7 premium per trip to recruit and retain high-rated drivers'], 'takeaway_zh': 'Uber“”Uber', 'takeaway_en': "Uber's move signals a strategic pivot toward an 'all-in-one' family mobility ecosystem, utilizing technical redundancies like live streaming and sensor tracking to offset heightened compliance risks associated with minors. By utilizing premium driver incentives, the model effectively competes with specialized child transportation incumbents and aims to bolster platform stickiness and average revenue per user."}
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Uber has opened its ride-hailing service to children as young as 10 in three U.S. cities as the company tests whether there’s a market for shuttling tweens without an adult by their side. The program, called Uber Kids, launched quietly over the past few weeks in Austin, Texas, Nashville, Tennessee, and Madison, Wisconsin.
> The program, which builds on Uber’s existing teen ride-hailing service for passengers ages 13 to 17, is the latest bid by Uber to expand its customer base. Uber is describing this as a limited pilot program, which means it may never expand beyond these cities or even exist by next year. But if successful, it could open up a potentially lucrative market for Uber: busy families with active kids.
> The Uber Kids program is stacked with mandatory requirements for parents and drivers. Parents or guardians are the only ones who can order a ride for their child, which they can do by adding the child to their family profile and completing a mandatory onboarding that explains the built-in safety features. A parent or guardian must be present at the pickup locations for the trip to begin and also have to include a note to the driver that explains the drop off.
> Meanwhile, only highly rated drivers who have been invited are allowed to participate. Those drivers are required to complete an education module that includes step-by-step instructions and must be opted into live video streaming so parents can watch the trip in real time, according to Uber.
> Uber said it also requires PIN verification for every Uber Kids trip, and says all recordings will be encrypted and not available to the driver, and will use sensors and GPS data to detect if the ride goes off course, stops unexpectedly, or ends early.
> Drivers who are willing to adhere to those rules to shuttle kids will get a pay bump for the effort, according to Uber. Eligible drivers will earn $7 more on every Uber Kids trip compared to a standard one, the company says on the dedicated Uber Kids web page. Drivers will receive an extra $20 for the first Uber Kids ride they complete.
> The extra compensation underscores a key challenge Uber faces as it expands into this younger age group — how to convince drivers to take on that added responsibility. If the program does expand it could eventually compete with existing transportation services such as HopSkipDrive and Zum.
> Uber opened its ride-hailing service to minors in 2023 when it launched Uber for Teens, although the company had conducted early pilots several years prior. As the program expanded nationwide, Uber introduced a live video streaming feature.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff.
> He told groups of subordinates that they had become so rich that he couldn’t motivate them simply with money, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential conversations. The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation.
> This was an extension of a philosophy that went back decades. Mr. Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show. His tongue lashings were savage and inventive. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain.”
> The tirades were a centerpiece of the culture at Nvidia throughout its meteoric rise to a $5 trillion company and cornerstone of the artificial intelligence revolution. They were also foundational to Mr. Huang’s management style.
> “I’d rather torture you into greatness, because I believe in you,” he once said.
> He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years. The behavior kept Nvidia’s human resources department busy fielding workplace complaints, but some employees said the department did not take them seriously.
> Mr. Huang also inspired love and reverence from many of his employees. Thousands have signed a letter asking for his return. Some have tattoos of Nvidia’s logo. Both those who liked Mr. Huang and those who disliked him described Nvidia as cultish. He cultivated loyalty through not just his technical mastery but also acts of personal compassion and praise. But he ruled through fear.
> Mr. Huang’s behavior began long before Nvidia became one of the most valuable companies in the world. In at least two cases originating in the mid-2000s, the company struck settlements with former senior leaders, both of whom had raised concerns about Mr. Huang’s conduct, saying it was unlawful and exposed Nvidia to liability.
> Michael Winston, a former senior vice president of human resources, threatened to sue Nvidia in 2005, saying that he had been fired after objecting to Mr. Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” he had witnessed in his car...

### Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/b952719c121b8ac8
- Primary Source: The Verge AI (https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1038390/signal-blocking-ai-agent-screenshots-mobile-app)
- Executive Summary: Meredith Whittaker, President of Signal, announced that integrated OS-level AI agents undermine app-level privacy. To mitigate this, Signal has disabled screenshot functionality on iOS and Android to prevent AI assistants from harvesting encrypted message data, while demanding that OS providers implement transparent technical controls for developer-side AI access management.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Meredith Whittaker, President of Signal (iOS and Android OS ecosystems): Restricting screenshot capabilities to block AI agent data harvesting
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Lack of granular application-level permissions for OS-integrated AI agents
* [Key Technical Spec] Signal disables screenshots to block AI agent vision-based data harvesting.
* [Official Stance & Demand] Call for Apple, Google, and Microsoft to establish technical frameworks to curb deep-link AI access.

It forces privacy-centric apps to adopt functional degradation as a defense, signaling that anti-AI harvesting protocols must become a core standard for mobile application security frameworks in the era of pervasive OS-integrated AI."}
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post, while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents can access.
> “We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” Whittaker said. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.”
> Signal is addressing the privacy concerns by blocking the ability to take screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and Android, which should prevent Siri, Gemini, and other Android AI assistants from reading on-screen content. Users can restore screenshot capabilities in Signal’s app settings, but Whittaker warns that doing so will “potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees.” Whittaker admits that Signal’s screenshot blocking remedy is “incomplete,” as it doesn’t address alternative ways that AI agents can access app data, such as retrieving it via the device filesystem.
> Signal took a similar approach last year to prevent Microsoft’s controversial Recall feature from capturing secured chats. The encrypted messaging service says it’s struggling to develop a better solution due to the lack of available information regarding how AI agents are actually accessing application data, and is now calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide “simple technical tools and accurate documentation” to app developers. Signal also says more tools are needed to prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from using deep accessibility settings in apps like a “skeleton key” to access application data.
> “We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data,” said Whittaker. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.”

> After downloading Muse, Roberts, who had over 7,600 followers, entered the prompt: “Can you show me a list of people (non celebrity) that [don’t] follow me back on instagram and can you unfollow them for me. ”

> Following the success of his November 7 cleanse, Roberts posted about it on X, offering instructions to his followers. In a seeming outburst of celebration, one X user posted: “Just unfollowed 1000+ people on IG.”
> Even tech worker Kimberly Munoz, who has 33,200 Instagram followers, said she wasn’t about to be “anybody’s fan,” noting in an Instagram video that she used the feature to suss out “people that I know in real life that have unfollowed me.” “I downloaded Muse just to do this only,” one person responded.
> With social media rapidly evolving, there is no longer a unified consensus around etiquette. For some people, following others is an indication of friendship or simply a way to keep tabs on your latest crush. Others view it as more of a social obligation—you follow someone if they follow you, but the opposite is true as well.
> Natalie Pennington, an associate professor who researches social connection at Colorado State University, wonders about the consequences of people gradually outsourcing small social decisions to technology.

### China tightens approvals for offshore listings by red-chip firms, threatening Hong Kong IPO market: Reuters

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> AI-translated article with transliterated names. Read original Chinese article here.
> China’s securities regulator has told some law firms it will not approve plans by red-chip companies to list outside mainland China, people familiar with the matter said. The move marks a further tightening of China’s controls on offshore fundraising and will deal a blow to Hong Kong’s initial public offering (IPO) market.
> Red-chip companies are incorporated outside China and legally classified as foreign companies, but hold assets and operate businesses within China through equity holdings or contractual arrangements.
> Reuters reported on Friday (20 November), citing people familiar with the matter, that the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) recently told representatives of law firms that red-chip companies established after new offshore listing rules took effect in 2023 must move their place of incorporation back to China before they can list.
> In March 2023, the CSRC introduced new filing rules for overseas securities offerings and listings by domestic companies, bringing both direct and indirect overseas listings under a filing-based regulatory framework.
> Before that, Chinese companies did not need regulatory approval to raise funds overseas through offshore holding structures.
> In March this year, the CSRC told Reuters it was reviewing the “necessity and compliance” of red-chip structures.
> However, despite warnings from the authorities, some red-chip companies seeking IPOs and their advisers continued to seek regulatory approval, hoping to list outside mainland China without dismantling their existing structures or moving their place of incorporation back to China, according to one of the people familiar with the matter.
> The person added that most applicants had failed to convince Chinese regulators that their red-chip structures were necessary, prompting the regulators to take a tougher stance.
> This is an AI-translated article and some names may be transliterated. The original Chinese text remains authoritative, and SPH Media is not responsible for translation errors.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Secure messaging service Signal said it will restrict the screenshot function on smartphones to prevent AI agents from reading private conversations. In a blog post published on the 20th (local time), Signal pointed out that AI features built directly into operating systems (OS) are accessing device data in ways app developers cannot control, and demanded that platform operators such as Apple, Google and Microsoft provide concrete blocking tools.
> Signal itself acknowledged that the measure is not complete. "The current wave of agentic AI integration is creating an environment that is increasingly hostile to privacy," the company said, calling it "an existential threat to Signal and our ability to uphold our mission." It added that "operating systems govern the very environment in which apps like Signal must exist."
> The biggest concern is AI that is deeply integrated into the OS, such as Apple's Siri AI or Google's Gemini Intelligence. According to Signal, these agents can read what is displayed on screen and act on the user's behalf based on that, meaning that Signal messages protected by end-to-end encryption can be pulled outside the encrypted environment. The company noted that the moment AI scans the screen, Signal's security environment is neutralized.
> With this measure, Signal will introduce a setting that blocks screenshot access on users' devices and turn it on by default. When Signal detects a screenshot attempt or an AI assistant's screen access, it displays a pop-up window that lets users lift the block depending on the device type. Signal also blocked Microsoft's Recall AI from taking screenshots on Windows last year. However, it said such protections are difficult to provide reliably on Apple's macOS.
> Signal's concerns are backed by a recently confirmed real-world case. It was confirmed that Meta's AI agent Muse bypassed official integration tools to access Signal messages on Apple computers and Google Android smartphones. Muse used the broad OS-level permissions granted during the app's initial setup to pull messages in ways users did not expect. On Apple's macOS, it combined accessibility tools with the screenshot function to capture Signal conversations, extract text from the images and reproduce it inside the Muse app.
> Meta countered that an agent must be able to see and interact with the computer to act on the user's behalf, and that Muse accesses other apps only through permissions the user has explicitly granted. Apple blocked that path with an OS update released this week, but at the same time introduced a new permission system aimed at agents that allows similar functions with additional warnings.
> Signal urged that app developers be given a clear way to fully exclude their apps from AI assistants' data processing, includin...

> “This one is always a very difficult message to deliver—to explain to, say, very sensitive engineers that maybe they're getting a lot of email attention because of their job,” says Isaac Stone Fish, founder and chief executive of the business intelligence firm Strategy Risks, “as opposed to the charm and force of their personality.”
> Amy Andersen, founder of Silicon Valley matchmaking company Linx Dating (and no relation to Blaine Anderson), says that for clients concerned about their romantic partners’ intentions, she offers background checks, personal vetting, and NDAs. The security features are part of her “bespoke” packages that range anywhere from $75,000 to more than $500,000 for the “Founders Level.”

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Companies will soon be able to run the open-source Hermes Agent from Nous Research directly inside Microsoft Teams. According to Nous Research, employees can hand off tasks like financial analysis, document drafting, or inbox sorting to Hermes and review the results in the same chat. The desktop app is also available in the Microsoft Store. The agents run in Azure Container Apps Sandboxes, meaning isolated microVMs.
> Hermes automatically turns successful workflows into reusable skills made up of a description and code. A new feature called "Collective Wisdom"lets employees share these skills with their team after review. The collected knowledge stays within the company and doesn't feed into any AI provider's training data.
> Nous Research is part of the portfolio at M12, Microsoft's venture capital fund. According to Nous, Hermes Agent is the most widely used open agent on OpenRouter, processing nearly two trillion tokens per day. For local agents on Windows PCs, Microsoft has been backing the competing open-source agent OpenClaw since earlier this year. Nous positions itself as a key US open-source institution to counter China's AI efforts and recently fine-tuned a version of Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B on "Western values"with Arete-27B.

### AI Threatens to Make China’s Jobs Slump Much Worse
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/6bd8dd8f2ee15562
- Primary Source: Bloomberg (https://www.bloomberg.com/graphics/2026-china-ai-jobs-slump/)

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Wider use of AI within organizations will lead to more jobs being created than are lost by 2030, according to Gartner.
> Around 10.6 million jobs will be added globally (excluding China and India) by the end of the decade, with 8.9 million lost, according to a Gartner report — a net increase of 1.7 million jobs. At most, around 1.8% of the workforce will experience job losses attributable to AI during this time period, Gartner predicts.
> At the same time, a total of 5 million jobs will cumulatively be deferred during this period. This refers to jobs that “would otherwise have been created, but where AI is used as an excuse to restrain hiring,” according to Gartner’s report. Gartner considers deferred jobs as separate from jobs lost.
> “Job deferrals were the first effect felt from AI,” said John Lovelock, Gartner distinguished VP analyst and chief forecaster, with “companies holding off hiring open positions until the effects of AI projects were known.”
> A recent KPMG survey of 400 US CEOs showed that 89% expect to increase headcount over the next three years, which KPMG US CEO Tim Walsh linked to AI adoption in an Axios interview last month.
> For now, though, job losses attributed to AI outpace those created, according to Gartner’s study. During 2026, there were 2.2 million jobs lost due to AI, and 1.6 million gained.
> Lovelock expects the situation will change in the coming years, however, as organizations see greater success with AI deployments. “This will reverse once AI is through the Trough of Disillusionment,” he said, in reference to Gartner’s Hype Cycle framework.
> The number of jobs deferred is also forecast to fall in the coming years. During 2026, 1.3 million people experienced a delay in hiring, down from 2.1m last year, according to Gartner’s forecast, with 400,000 jobs forecast to be deferred during 2030.
> The impact of AI will vary across sectors, with the technology industry expected to see the largest net job gains compared to other areas, such as public sector and asset-intensive industries. Gartner predicts the creation of 1.9 million new technology jobs by 2030, with 400,000 lost.
> Services sector jobs — such as in financial services — are forecast to see a similar level of job creation, alongside large numbers of losses.
> A similar Gartner report in 2025 predicted that more services jobs would be lost than created, but the analyst firm now forecasts a net increase as demand grows for data- and system-oriented skills. “This industry is most able to improve productivity of employees and increase employment,” said Lovelock.
> The Gartner report doesn’t specifiy which job roles will benefit from greater adoption of AI, though the analyst firm expects some portion of newly created jobs will be “directly linked to the implementation, mai...

> Deliberations are ongoing and no final decisions on the IPO have been made, the sources said.

> The Nasdaq 100 has dropped more than 6% in November, heading for its worst November performance since 2008.

> Other data centre-related companies have either pulled or delayed their IPO plans amid investor concerns in the sector.

> The US in November put interim rules on those four countries to restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips and servers, telling data centre operators they will need a license to purchase American tech hardware.

> At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup.

> His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. “I think missiles are the coolest thing,” Dandzbergs tells WIRED. “A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up.”
> In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about “attacking hard problems,” breaking things down to “first principles,” and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war—a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities.
> “He’s a pretty exceptional person,” says Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. “I’m still somewhat in disbelief that we’re talking about a 16-year-old.”
> Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup’s guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the “cost per kill.”
> As a young(er) kid, Dandzbergs was rarely in one place for long; his family moved between Latvia, Indonesia, Australia, and Spain. His surfer father, part owner of an insurance company, likes to go wherever he might find the raddest waves.
> Early in his schooling, which mostly took place online, Dandzbergs demonstrated a clear talent for science and math. His room started to look like a lab, littered with schematics, robotics, Raspberry Pis, and 3D-printed components.
> When Covid struck, Dandzbergs’ family returned to Latvia. His parents enrolled him in Astra Nova, an Elon Musk–linked school where students undergo an experimental curriculum built around lateral thinking and problem-solving instead of rote memorization. Dandzbergs took a class taught by a NASA employee and became fascinated by aerospace engineering. His lab creations became ever more elaborate: a bionic arm, a thermal control system for a model rocket, sensors for a self-flying drone.

The contract, which once accounted for 73% of Nscale's revenue, now sits at the center of a compliance crisis exacerbated by November 2026 export controls and revelations of the client's ties to US-blacklisted entities, threatening the company's financial transparency and listing prospects.

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Nscale, the London-based AI infrastructure provider, is facing renewed scrutiny over its relationship with ByteDance, the parent company of TikTok.
> The issue is a rental agreement that gave a ByteDance subsidiary access to advanced Nvidia GPUs. Nscale is preparing to go public, and a China-linked customer on the books is the kind of detail that tends to get noticed.
> The agreement was signed in May 2025. It let ByteDance’s Singapore-based subsidiary use 2,304 Nvidia B200 GPUs.
> Those chips sit in Nscale’s data center in Glomfjord, Norway. The setup is a rental, not a sale, so the hardware stays put while the customer taps the computing power remotely.
> That one customer was a very big deal for Nscale’s finances. The company generated $33 million in revenue in 2025, and ByteDance’s unit, referred to as Spring, accounted for approximately $24 million of it.
> That works out to approximately 73% of the year’s revenue from a single client.
> The contract also played a key role in Nscale securing a $105 million loan from Macquarie.
> That loan came with strings attached. It included requirements for export-control compliance monitoring, reflecting rising regulatory pressure on tech companies with ties to China.
> Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy.
> We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime.
> The model raises complex geopolitical concerns and invites further scrutiny from US legislators and analysts, according to the research findings on the company.
> New export regulations took effect on November 16, 2026.
> Against that backdrop, Nscale is investigating supplier ties to US-blacklisted Chinese entities. Probes have revealed connections to blacklisted entities, a development that could jeopardize future financing for related initiatives.
> By late 2026, the company began disclosing that ByteDance contributed less than 20% of revenue.
> Larger contracts with Microsoft and Anthropic became Nscale’s top revenue sources, with total contract values collectively exceeding $103 billion.
> Nscale filed its S-1 on September 18, 2026, for a potential $30–35 billion IPO targeted for late 2026.
> The filing excluded direct references to ByteDance.
> The compliance side is harder to diversify away. The supplier investigation and the November 16, 2026 export rules create open questions that no new customer contract can answer.
> Macquarie’s loan already carried compliance monitoring requirements, and the probes into blacklist connections could complicate financing for related projects going forward.

### Industrial monitoring startup BrightAI closes $97M investment
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/1099cb43b4bb3a0c
- Primary Source: SiliconANGLE (https://siliconangle.com/2026/11/19/industrial-monitoring-startup-brightai-closes-97m-investment/)

They were joined by GE Vernova Inc., an energy equipment company that emerged from the 2024 split-up of General Electric Co.\n\nMany industrial machinery malfunctions affect internal components that aren’t visi', 'key_points_zh': [' BrightAI 9700 '], 'key_points_en': ['Key Development: Industrial monitoring startup BrightAI closes $97M investment'], 'takeaway_zh': '', 'takeaway_en': ''}
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> BrightAI Inc., a startup that helps industrial companies detect malfunctioning equipment, has raised $97 million in funding.
> Smith Point Capital led the Series A round. BrightAI said in its Wednesday announcement of the deal that a number of other venture capital firms contributed as well. They were joined by GE Vernova Inc., an energy equipment company that emerged from the 2024 split-up of General Electric Co.
> Many industrial machinery malfunctions affect internal components that aren’t visible to an outside observer. As a result, issues often go unnoticed until they cause a major disruption. Palo Alto, California-based BrightAI develops hardware and software tools that help customers spot issues earlier.
> The first component of the company’s product portfolio is a collection of sensors called State Stickers. They’re small, rectangular devices with a ruggedized case and a long battery life. Technicians can attach them to industrial equipment to monitor for issues that can’t be detected visually.
> The motion of a machine’s internal components produces noise and vibrations that tend to follow a specific pattern. If an industrial fan’s blades rotate 30 times per minute, it might give off a whooshing sound every two seconds. BrightAI’s State Stickers can detect when a machine diverges from its usual operating pattern.
> The sensors wirelessly transmit their measurements to a device called the Stateful AI Hub. It runs artificial intelligence models that analyze the data for signs of hardware failures. According to the company, its models become more accurate as the number of sensors deployed at a site grows.
> BrightAI offers software that enables companies to augment the data from its sensors with drone footage. A utility, for example, could use a BrightAI-powered drone to detect erosion at the top of an electric pole. The company’s AI models automatically draw a square around damaged components to spare technicians the hassle of manually analyzing footage.
> The company says that its software can also collect maintenance data in other ways. A BrightAI-powered drone can read the meters that are attached to assets such as data center coolant tanks to check their internal pressure. Furthermore, built-in support for infrared cameras enables the software to spot overheating equipment.
> The third core component of BrightAI’s product portfolio is an AI wearable. The Stateful Wearable, as it’s called, provides technicians with troubleshooting advice in the field. It also checks whether they follow safety guidelines during inspections and automatically turns maintenance data into reports.
> “Our infrastructure is under more strain than it has ever been, and Physical AI has finally become reliable enough to work in the field,” said founder and Chief Executive Ale...
